issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking eviction for use beyond the leased purpose must plead and prove the change through proper evidence; a tenant’s qualified explanation does not by itself establish that change.
material_facts: The landlord alleged that premises leased for residence had recently been put to another use but gave no particulars of the alleged change.
The tenant denied changing the use and explained that office files were sometimes handled at home in one room that was also used by family members as a study room.
The landlord did not establish that the premises functioned as an office, and the lower authorities treated the tenant’s explanation as an admission and expected the tenant to prove a negative.
issues.conclusion: The alleged change of use was not established, so the eviction ground could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13(2)(ii)(b) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, the landlord must plead and establish by proper evidence that the tenant used the premises for a purpose other than the one for which they were leased. The tenant does not bear the burden of proving the negative. A written statement must be read as a whole and in context, rather than treating a fragment of a qualified explanation as an admission.

rule.if: change_of_use_eviction_proceeding and (allegation_lacks_particulars or evidence_does_not_support_change) and tenant_denies_change

predicates.change_of_use_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction on the basis that the tenant used the premises for a purpose other than the leased purpose.
predicates.allegation_lacks_particulars: The landlord alleges a change of use without specifying the relevant details of that change.
predicates.evidence_does_not_support_change: The evidence does not establish that the tenant changed the use of the premises.
predicates.tenant_denies_change: The tenant denies changing the use and gives an explanation that does not amount to an admission of the alleged change.

issues.definition: When eviction is sought for a change of use, an unparticularized allegation or insufficient supporting evidence, together with the tenant’s denial, means the eviction ground is not established.

issues.legal_issue: Incidental personal work or family study in one room of a residence does not change the premises’ residential use when the premises remain occupied as a home and no regular commercial or public-facing office operates there.
material_facts: The building was let for residence and continued to be occupied by the tenant’s managing director and his family.
One room contained office files and equipment used for occasional work at home and was also used by family members for study.
There was no evidence that company business was regularly conducted there, that transactions took place there, or that officials, customers, or members of the public visited it as an office.
The lease did not specifically prohibit using a room for study or occasional work at home.
issues.conclusion: The incidental use of the room did not change the use or character of the building, which remained residential.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(b), read with the definitions of non-residential, residential, and scheduled buildings in Sections 2(d), 2(g), and 2(h) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, requires a change in the use of the building, assessed purposively and on the facts. Gurdial Batra v. Raj Kumar Jain supports the view that a small change that does not cause mischief or detriment to the landlord’s property is not necessarily actionable; Section 108(o) of the Transfer of Property Act is noted in that context. Bishamber Dass Kohli v. Satya Bhalla concerned an established lawyer’s office that changed the building’s character to a scheduled building and is distinguishable from occasional personal work at home. M. Arul Jothi v. Lajja Bal involved a specific lease prohibition and is likewise distinguishable. Each case must be decided on its pleadings and evidence.

predicates.change_of_use_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction on the basis that the tenant used the premises for a purpose other than the leased purpose.
predicates.residential_occupancy_continued: The tenant and family continued to occupy the premises as a home.
predicates.one_room_used_for_personal_homework_or_f: One room was used for occasional work at home or family study rather than as a separate business establishment.
predicates.no_regular_commercial_or_public_office_a: No regular business activity or public-facing office operated from the premises.

issues.definition: Where residential occupancy continues, use of one room for personal work or family study without regular commercial or public-facing office activity does not change the premises’ residential character.
